citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (2014). Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. ECCV 2014.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (Microsoft Research, Cornell NYC Tech, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, Facebook AI Research, Brown University, California Institute of Technology, University of California at Irvine)
description: MS COCO is a large-scale dataset for object detection and instance segmentation containing 91 common object categories with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328,000 images of complex everyday scenes. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentation masks to aid in precise object localization. The dataset emphasizes non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships between objects.
name: Microsoft COCO (MS COCO)
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker per instance segmentation (with 3–5 workers for verification)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality on category labeling was analyzed by comparing AMT workers to seven expert workers (co-authors). The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert. Worker recall saturates at around 9–10 AMT workers. Over 99% of all object categories are estimated to be detected given 8 annotators. Workers below a precision threshold had all their work rejected.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline had three stages: (1) Category Labeling — workers used a hierarchical interface to identify which of 91 object categories were present in each image, with 8 workers per image; (2) Instance Spotting — workers placed crosses on all instances of each identified category, with 8 workers per image; (3) Instance Segmentation — workers drew precise polygon segmentation masks around each object instance, with a training task required per category and a verification step by 3–5 workers per segmentation.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was deliberately designed to reduce iconic-image bias by collecting non-iconic images from Flickr using pairwise object category queries. The paper acknowledges that including difficult (non-iconic) images during training may not always help, as such examples may act as noise. The dataset only includes "thing" categories and not "stuff" categories, which may limit contextual information.
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairs of object categories (e.g., "dog + car") and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Photographs collected from Flickr, searched using pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images containing common objects in natural contexts.
rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release is limited to 80 of the 91 categories (11 categories omitted due to too many instances, ambiguity, difficulty of labeling, confusion with other categories, or too few instances). Only "thing" categories are labeled, not "stuff" categories. Dense crowds of objects are labeled as a single crowd segment rather than individually.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For images containing more than 10–15 instances of a given category, remaining instances were marked as "crowds" using a single (possibly multi-part) segment rather than individually segmented. Areas marked as crowds are ignored during evaluation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were detected and removed across dataset splits. Images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates. An AMT filtering task removed invalid or iconic images from the candidate set. Segmentations that did not receive at least 4 of 5 favorable votes in verification were discarded and the corresponding instances returned to the unsegmented pool.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two roughly equal parts released in 2014 and 2015. MS COCO is described as evolving and growing over time, with up-to-date information available on the project website.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance the state-of-the-art in object recognition and scene understanding, enabling more capable computer vision systems that can recognize objects in natural, non-iconic contexts as they appear in everyday life.
rai:dataUseCases: Object detection, instance segmentation, semantic scene understanding, contextual reasoning between objects, precise 2D object localization, image captioning, and benchmarking of recognition algorithms.

evidence.name: The Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) dataset contains 91 common object categories with 82 of them having more than 5,000 labeled instances
evidence.description: The Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) dataset contains 91 common object categories with 82 of them having more than 5,000 labeled instances, Fig. 6. In total the dataset has 2,500,000 labeled instances in 328,000 images.
evidence.url: To download and learn more about MS COCO please see the project website2. MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online. 2. http://mscoco.org/
evidence.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin Michael Maire Serge Belongie Lubomir Bourdev Ross Girshick James Hays Pietro Perona Deva Ramanan C. Lawrence Zitnick Piotr Dollár
evidence.publisher: Funding for all crowd worker tasks was provided by Microsoft.
evidence.datePublished: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images
evidence.inLanguage: We added five written caption descriptions to each image in MS COCO. A full description of the caption statistics and how they were gathered will be provided shortly in a separate publication.
evidence.citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick, "Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context," in ECCV, 2014.
evidence.isLiveDataset: MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation. A search for "dog" will tend to return iconic images of large, centered dogs. However, if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as "dog + car" we found many more non-iconic images.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT). Our user interfaces are described in detail in the appendix.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline is outlined in Fig. 3. For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT). Our user interfaces are described in detail in the appendix. Note that, since the original version of this work, we have taken a number of steps to further improve the quality of the annotations. In particular, we have increased the number of annotators for the category labeling and instance spotting stages to eight. We also added a stage to verify the instance segmentations.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image. A category is considered present if any worker indicated the category; false positives are handled in subsequent stages.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We analyzed crowd worker quality on the category labeling task by comparing to dedicated expert workers, see Fig. 4(a). We compared precision and recall of seven expert workers (co-authors of the paper) with the results obtained by taking the union of one to ten AMT workers. Ground truth was computed using majority vote of the experts. Fig. 4(a) shows that the union of 8 AMT workers, the same number as was used to collect our labels, achieved greater recall than any of the expert workers.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After 10-15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, the remaining instances were marked as "crowds" using a single (possibly multi-part) segment. For the purpose of evaluation, areas marked as crowds will be ignored and not affect a detector's score.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We introduced a new dataset for detecting and segmenting objects found in everyday life in their natural environments. Utilizing over 70,000 worker hours, a vast collection of object instances was gathered, annotated and organized to drive the advancement of object detection and segmentation algorithms.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Our goal was to collect a dataset such that a majority of images are non-iconic, Fig. 2(c). It has been shown that datasets containing more non-iconic images are better at generalizing. We collected non-iconic images using two strategies.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Note that we have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories. We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances).
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context.
evidence.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: To accommodate a faster release schedule, we split the MS COCO dataset into two roughly equal parts. The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015. MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.
